articles.summary: The director has turned Kazuo Ishiguro’s acclaimed novel about an ailing adolescent and her glitchy robot friend into a thought-provoking film. What do the pair think this story says about tech, love and grief?
body: I n the wings of the London film festival, a group of young influencers are discussing their personal highlights. Klara and the Sun, says one, and her colleagues agree. It’s not just that the film is still so fresh in their memory, or that they have gathered today to meet its creators and stars. Klara is funny and moving; it’s their festival favourite so far. I relay this exchange to Taika Waititi, the film’s director, who is sipping bottled water in a room down the hall. His gaze widens. He almost chokes. “Thank God!” he exclaims with just a bit too much heat.

articles.title: Sebastian Koch, Toni Servillo Set for Oscar Winner Gabriele Salvatores’ Chess-World Noir ‘The Lüneburg Variation’ (EXCLUSIVE)
articles.summary: Sebastian Koch, star of Oscar-winning German film “The Lives of Others,” and Toni Servillo, protagonist of Italy’s Oscar winner “The Great Beauty,” are set to topline “The Lüneburg Variation,” a noir based in the world of chess, directed by Gabriele Salvatores.
body: The book opens with the suicide of a wealthy Munich businessman named Dieter Frisch near Vienna, leading to flashbacks of a revenge plot orchestrated through the game of chess.

“It is the story of a duel that lasts more than 40 years, fought by two adversaries on the battlefield of a chessboard. Chess! The most violent sport in existence and, perhaps, the least cinematic. It’s a great challenge, and one I was happy to take on,” Salvatores said in a statement.
The director added that he would delve into “the violent, magical, esoteric and mysterious dimension of chess, that is, instead, truly cinematic!”
“Maurensig envisioned a film of half-light; darkness and fire. Compelling and cruel. I hope I can deliver just that…,” Salvatores went on to note.

articles.title: ‘The History Boys’ Returns to London West End After 20 Years, With Nicholas Hytner Back Directing Alan Bennett’s Play
articles.summary: Alan Bennett’s “The History Boys” is going back to London’s West End after a 20-year absence. Nicholas Hytner returns to the National Theatre production he first staged in 2004, which later went to Broadway and won six Tony Awards there.
body: Alan Bennett ’s “ The History Boys ” is going back to London’s West End after a 20-year absence.

Hytner is producing with Brian and Dayna Lee, whose credits include “Giant.” That play won the Olivier for best new play and earned four Tony nominations on Broadway with John Lithgow. The three most recently partnered on “The Standard of Living.” Len Blavatnik and Danny Cohen also produce for Access Entertainment, with Mark Rubinstein as executive producer.
The Lees said it was a privilege to return Bennett’s play to the West End with “the incomparable Nicholas Hytner once again at the helm.”
After its 2004 bow at the National, the play transferred to both the West End and Broadway. It won three Olivier Awards as well as the six Tonys, and its young ensemble went on to break out.

body: Malaysia’s Wong Kew Soon produced “Snow in Midsummer,” which won the Firebird Award for best film at the Hong Kong International Film Festival. He now develops films and documentaries through Studio Forty-Five Hundred.

Singapore has two producers in the lineup. Sam Chua Weishi’s recent feature credits include Rafael Manuel’s “Filipiñana,” which played Sundance this year, and Nelicia Low’s Karlovy Vary title “Pierce.” Wendy Lie’s latest, Nelson Yeo’s “The House on the Moon,” competed at Locarno. Her first feature, Ang Geck Geck’s “Ah Girl,” took a special jury prize at Rotterdam this year.

articles.title: Netflix, Bengali Streamer Hoichoi Partner to Bring Series to Hindi, Tamil and Telugu Audiences
articles.summary: Every series Bengali streamer Hoichoi launches over the next two years will get Hindi, Tamil and Telugu-language versions streaming exclusively on Netflix, under a partnership the two companies unveiled in Mumbai on Thursday.
body: The two companies will also make new shows together. Netflix and Hoichoi will work on original series that rework selected Hoichoi stories, with Hoichoi Studios producing. The companies said each adaptation would bring in new creative voices. Further details have yet to be revealed.

For Netflix, the pact is part of a wider effort to supplement its originals with more licensed programming from outside producers. The streamer said its global audience, which it puts at close to a billion people, gives studios, networks and creators a strong reason to work with it.

The Hoichoi pact follows two other high-profile licensing moves. In France, Netflix now carries the full programming lineup of broadcaster TF1. In Brazil, Netflix struck a deal earlier this month with broadcaster Globo, which had long held out from licensing to the streamer in its home market even as its content appeared on Netflix elsewhere in Latin America and around the world.

articles.title: Dame Judi Dench: 'I can't do a play, a film or read any more'
articles.summary: Dame Judi Dench tells BBC Radio 4's Today programme about how her eye condition has affected her life.
body: Oscar-winning actress Dame Judi Dench says her eye condition has left her unable to perform on stage or read, more than a decade after she was diagnosed.
Dame Judi was diagnosed with age-related macular degeneration (AMD) in 2012, a condition that affects her vision and has made it incredibly difficult to even recognise faces.
Speaking to Emma Barnett on BBC Radio 4's Today programme, she said: "I can't be on stage. I can't do a play any more. I can't do a film any more. I can't read any more."
She also revealed how her condition can lead to awkward encounters, saying she sometimes approaches the wrong people "and give them an almost hug" before realising her mistake.

articles.title: ‘A vehicle to expose prejudice, bias, and stupidity’: Sacha Baron Cohen defends Ali G as satire
articles.summary: The actor defended his new film, Ali G: Who Iz I?, saying his aim is to bring people ‘face-to-face with the danger of fanaticism and conspiracy theories’ Sacha Baron Cohen has launched an impassioned defence of satire, the right to offend, and his Ali G character on in a lengthy article for Time…
body: On the eve of the release of his new film, Ali G: Who Iz I?, Baron Cohen described satire as “more important than ever”, adding that “along the way, some people, instead of laughing, wince or worse, take offence.”

Comparing modern satirists to the traditional figure of the “bouffon”, Baron Cohen described satire as “the humour of the dispossessed … using biting and at times cruel humour to undermine systemic injustice”.

Having previously released films containing controversial characters including Kazakh journalist Borat Sagdiyev, Austrian fashion show presenter Brüno Gehard, and a thinly disguised Colonel Gaddafi parody called Admiral General Aladeen, Baron Cohen directly took on critics of the Ali G character, who has been criticised in the past for laughing at black street culture and described as a “black caricature”.

Baron Cohen writes: “I made this latest film for the same reason I’ve always done this work. Not only to make people laugh, but also to bring them face-to-face with the danger of fanaticism and conspiracy theories.”

articles.title: ‘Nobody Wants This’ Season 3 Review: Kristen Bell and Adam Brody’s Netflix Romance Levels Up but Can’t Ditch Old Habits
articles.summary: Justine Lupe, Timothy Simons and Jackie Tohn also return, as the central couple — a rabbi and a former agnostic preparing to convert to Judaism — take a big step forward in their relationship.
body: If nothing else, give Nobody Wants This credit for allowing itself a tiny bit of growth: After two seasons of exhaustingly circular conflict about whether a good-boy rabbi like Noah ( Adam Brody ) could ever really be with an agnostic Gentile sex podcaster like Joanne ( Kristen Bell ), season three begins not only with the couple moving in together, but Joanne starting Jewish conversion classes.

Admittedly, it does feel good to bask for once in what feels right about Joanne and Noah’s relationship rather than fret over what might be wrong about it. The lovebirds are so giddy they wake each other up in the middle of the night just to coo: “Hey. We live together.” Nothing can pierce their romantic bliss, not even minor annoyances like Joanne’s inability to ever shut a cabinet door (“It’s like living with a ghost,” Noah complains adorably) or bigger ones like her almost sabotaging their first trip as a couple when she runs into a desperately needy fan (creator Erin Foster ) at the airport.

articles.title: ‘I’m always being real’: what on earth persuades disgraced people like Elizabeth Holmes to let the cameras in?
articles.summary: With You Can See Everything, Holmes joins other such high-profile subjects as Lance Armstrong, Imelda Marcos and Anthony Weiner to allow film-makers to document their lives. But do they ever come out well?
body: That question of authenticity is at the heart of documentary film-making. You Can See Everything is as much about the ambiguous relationship between film-maker and subject as it is about Holmes herself. There is often a power struggle over narrative control in documentaries, with both sides of the dynamic wanting different outcomes from the final film. Watching You Can See Everything inevitably prompts the question: why would Holmes, days before she heads to jail, invite the scrutiny of a film crew?

Some people, like Holmes, think a documentary will help rebuild their reputation after public disgrace. When Anthony Weiner, who resigned from Congress after tweeting a photo of his bulging groin, tried to stage a professional comeback with a New York mayoral bid, he allowed cameras to film the journey. Only, he had more to hide: when further sex scandals emerged, his campaign went from a story of public redemption to innuendo-laden humiliation. And all the while, the cameras kept rolling. Weiner is a prime example of a subject losing control of the narrative.

articles.title: Canal+ Touts ‘Les Mis,’ ‘Shaun the Sheep,’ ‘Pressure’ Box Office, Warns of Impact of French VAT Proposal
articles.summary: “2026 is shaping up to be a landmark year for StudioCanal," CEO Maxime Saada says.
body: “2026 is shaping up to be a landmark year for StudioCanal, with strong box-office performances from Pressure and the recent releases Les Misérables, The Doll ( Lalka ) and the third Shaun the Sheep film,” Canal+ Group CEO Maxime Saada said on Thursday in providing a revenue update for the company. “Our bold and diverse slate includes Ink, which opened the Venice Film Festival, Elsinore, winner of the International People’s Choice Award at the Toronto International Film Festival, and the highly anticipated Violette ( Changer l’eau des fleurs ).”

Content Production, Distribution and Other revenue for the January-September period increased by 9.3 percent to €530 million ($596 million) on a restated basis, or by 5.4 percent on a like-for-like basis. “This was mainly driven by StudioCanal’s strong box office performance and international sales, as well as its increased scale following the acquisition of Lucky Red in February 2026,” the company said. Streamer Dailymotion was “negatively impacted by lower advertising in the third quarter, against a challenging market backdrop.”

articles.title: Four locations in the running to be UK City of Culture 2029
articles.summary: The winner, announced in early 2027, will receive £10m to deliver a year of cultural activities.
body: Blackpool, Milton Keynes, Sheffield and Wrexham have been shortlisted to become the UK's City of Culture in 2029.
The winning location will be announced in May and will be the fifth holder of the title - following Derry-Londonderry, Hull, Coventry and Bradford.
A different location is given the City of Culture title every four years. Each shortlisted city will now receive at least £125,000 from the government to do further work on their bid.
The eventual winner will receive £10m to deliver a year of cultural events and activities drawing on its "local strengths and stories".
